Will my hon. friend be good enough to give us a list of the articles and the points of shipment ?

Take agricultural implements, the present rate from Montreal or Toronto to Vancouver or Victoria, is $1.38 per hundred pounds. Prom Boston and New York it is only $1.30, and from Buffalo, Pittsburg or Chicago it is also $1.30. Then take pianos and organs, the present rate is $2.43 per 100 pounds from Montreal or Toronto to Victoria or Vancouver, and from Boston and New York to these same ports it is only $2.25. And from Boston and New York to Seattle or Tacoma, the rate is still lower, $2.20 per 100 pounds, against $2.43 over our own Canadian road. On rubber boots and shoes, scales, sewing machines, stoves, furnaces, radiators, wagons, windmills, woodenware, &c\, the freight is from 15 cents to 20 cents per 100 pounds more to Victoria and Vancouver from Montreal or Toronto than if they were shipped from Boston or New York over American roads. It is in fact a scandal and an outrage that railways built by Canadian money should be in a position to charge so much for carrying these goods. Take 20 cents per 100 pounds on 40,000 pounds, and that amounts to $80 per carload, which would go a long way towards paying the duty the Americans are charged on their goods. This state of things we cannot hope to remedy until we have our own transcontinental line. We will then be able to place our manufactures on the same plane as the Americans, which is an additional reason why we should proceed without delay in building this now line.

Having shown that this new line is a necessity, I wish to say a word or two on the route selected.
Before the hon. gentleman passes from this point, would he be kind enough to give us the lines on which he says these cheaper rates are charged ?
The American lines running out to the coast and thence by water to Vancouver and Victoria.

We desire to build up this Dominion into a great and glorious part of the British empire, to bind the several provinces and territories together not with a rope of sand, but with bonds that can never be broken. In that work we can be greatly helped by a real national railway. We have such a railway running through two of the provinces and part of a third. I have been looking through the county of Colchester and mingling with these men who come to the fences with their forks in their hands and leaning on their forks give me more instruction in five minutes than any cabinet minister can give me in an hour. I have been over the county of Colchester listening to the remarks of Liberals and Conservatives alike.
In these journeyings, I met many constituents of my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Russell), and I can tell him, that it would be better for him to visit his county, than to be talking here about the city of St. John, for if he visits Hants, he will find a panic in that county that menaces his future political life.

I delight in the amenities of debate. I think nothing is gained by roughness of expression in this House, and therefore, I want to congratulate the Solicitor General on the splendid way in which he uses the English language. He uses it with precision, and as I am a little bit of a student of that language, I tell him, he uses the language with great grace and force, and I wish to commend his example to the English speaking people on his side of the House. They can improve their speech making by copying the English language, which the Solicitor General, though it is not his mother tongue, uses. I made my argument on the Grand Trunk question last year, and I do not intend to repeat it. I abide by that argument. It may not have been on all fours with the argument made by many members of this House, but I am persuaded that it will be the argument that ultimately (when the people thoroughly understand this whole matter) will defeat this government at the polls.
